title: The Five Engines: Segment Economics & Real-World Customer Walkthroughs

epigraph.quote: A facilities contract looks identical from thirty thousand feet, yet the economics of mopping a suburban school are worlds apart from commissioning a data center microgrid.
epigraph.author: Industrial Operations Maxim

web_blocks.html: To understand ABM Industries, investors cannot evaluate its $8,745.9 million of FY2025 revenue as a monolith [1]. The company operates five distinct divisions [1]. Operating margins span from 5.8% in Aviation to 9.4% in Manufacturing & Distribution [1]. Corporate unallocated expenses totaled $370.5 million in FY2025 [1]. These corporate overhead costs fund enterprise IT systems, executive leadership, legal counsel, and shared back-office services [1]. Before these overhead allocations, the five operating segments generated $687.7 million in combined operating profit [1].

web_blocks.caption: Table 2.1: ABM Industries Segment Revenue & Operating Profit Mix (FY2025 Audited 10-K)
web_blocks.takeaway: Manufacturing & Distribution (9.4%) and Technical Solutions (9.0%) deliver the highest segment margins, while B&I still provides over half of segment operating dollars. Heavy corporate overhead ($370.5M) compresses consolidated GAAP operating margin to 3.7% [1, 17].

web_blocks.html: 1. Business & Industry (B&I — $4,126.0M Revenue, 7.7% Margin): B&I is ABM's flagship commercial engine [1]. It serves Class A office towers, sports arenas, financial institutions, and retail campuses [1, 13]. Real-world customer example: Consider a multi-tenant Class A skyscraper in downtown San Francisco or New York City. The property owner faces fragmented oversight across nightly janitorial crews, stationary HVAC engineers, and underground parking attendants. ABM consolidates these functions under a multi-year Integrated Facility Solutions (IFS) contract [7, 18]. The base contract typically bills as a fixed monthly fee per square foot [18]. Unionized facility engineering often prices on a cost-plus structure [7, 18]. Separate 'tag work' billing covers tenant improvements, event cleanups, and emergency repairs [7, 18]. Hybrid office attendance curtailed daily floor occupancy and dampened discretionary tag work in FY2024–FY2025 [13, 19]. Even so, ABM's focus on trophy office assets and sports stadiums helped B&I post ~2% growth late in FY2025 [13, 19].

2. Manufacturing & Distribution (M&D — $1,618.6M Revenue, 9.4% Margin): M&D represents ABM's highest-margin division, delivering a 9.4% operating margin [1]. The segment services automotive factories, e-commerce fulfillment centers, pharmaceutical laboratories, and semiconductor fabrication facilities [1, 12]. Real-world customer example: A Tier-1 semiconductor fabrication plant in the US Southwest cannot tolerate particulate contamination or unscheduled cleanroom downtime. In February 2026, ABM acquired WGNSTAR for $275 million in an all-cash transaction [12]. Following this deal, ABM embeds specialized technicians directly inside customer fabs [12]. Crews manage cleanroom protocols, chemical and specialty gas delivery systems, and production tool maintenance [12]. This specialized work carries contractual technical service level agreements or dedicated headcount retainers [12]. Client switching costs remain high because cleaning failures risk millions of dollars in scrapped silicon wafers.

3. Aviation ($1,118.7M Revenue, 5.8% Margin): Aviation delivers passenger mobility assistance, aircraft cabin cleaning, baggage support, parking operations, and shuttle transit [1, 20]. Real-world customer example: At Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), ABM manages remote employee parking lots and high-frequency shuttle transit [20]. In the United Kingdom, the firm recently launched a major multi-service engagement at London Heathrow Airport [20, 21]. Aviation contracts represent multi-year public or airline-consortium tenders [1, 7]. These pacts enforce strict SLA performance penalties and involve unionized labor, explaining the modest 5.8% margin [1, 7]. However, rising global passenger traffic supported rapid top-line growth [4, 15]. Aviation revenue expanded 20% YoY in Q2 FY2026 [15]. Segment revenue grew 12.5% YoY to $328.1 million in Q3 FY2026 [4].

4. Technical Solutions (ATS — $960.6M Revenue, 9.0% Margin): ATS represents ABM's specialized engineering division [10, 11]. It deploys RavenVolt microgrids, Quality Uptime Services UPS maintenance, EV charging hubs, and electrical retrofits [10, 11]. Real-world customer example: A hyperscale data center developer facing multi-year utility interconnect queues hires ABM and RavenVolt on an EPC contract [10, 22]. ABM engineers single-line electrical schematics and fabricates custom UL-listed medium-voltage switchgear [10, 22]. Crews install hybrid natural-gas generation, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems (BESS) [10, 22]. Quality Uptime technicians subsequently deliver recurring preventive UPS maintenance [11, 22]. Because EPC milestones hinge on customer site readiness and utility approvals, quarterly revenue fluctuates [4, 15]. Segment revenue surged 27% YoY in Q2 FY2026 [15]. Growth then moderated to 4.2% ($259.9 million) in Q3 FY2026 due to client project deferrals [4, 15].

5. Education ($922.0M Revenue, 7.3% Margin): Established through the 2017 GCA Services acquisition, Education serves K-12 public districts and universities [1, 8]. Real-world customer example: A suburban K-12 district facing 25% custodial turnover and deferred HVAC maintenance selects ABM on a 3-to-5-year contract [8, 23]. ABM manages daily classroom sanitation, athletic groundskeeping, and boiler and chiller operations [8, 23]. Contracts generally feature fixed pricing with annual CPI or statutory minimum-wage escalation clauses [8, 23]. This commercial model generates steady, non-cyclical 2%–3% organic growth, including +2% YoY in Q2 FY2026 [15, 23].

web_blocks.title: SEGMENT MIX SHIFT: WHY 9% MARGINS IN M&D AND ATS MATTER
paragraphs: Every $100 million of revenue shifted from Aviation (5.8% margin) or Education (7.3%) into M&D (9.4%) or ATS (9.0%) creates $1.7 million to $3.6 million in operating profit [1]. This margin differential guides management's capital allocation strategy [1, 11, 12]. ABM deployed $118M for Quality Uptime in 2024 and $275M for WGNSTAR in 2026 [11, 12]. These deals prioritize high-value engineering over commoditized commercial office janitorial books [11, 12].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand why ABM Industries trades and operates the way it does, you have to stop looking at the consolidated income statement for a moment and walk the floor of each of its five operating segments. On paper, all five businesses 'maintain facilities.' On the ground, their economics, customer psychology, and switching costs could not be more different.

Start with Business & Industry, the $4.13 billion giant that still accounts for nearly half of ABM's revenue. Picture a 50-story Class A office tower in downtown Manhattan or San Francisco. The real estate investment trust that owns the building does not want to hire 80 night cleaners, 12 licensed stationary engineers to babysit the basement chillers, and 15 parking attendants—nor does it want to negotiate directly with local labor unions. So it signs a multi-year Integrated Facility Solutions contract with ABM. ABM collects a predictable monthly fee, and whenever a corporate tenant renovates a floor or hosts a major event, ABM bills high-margin 'tag work' on top. The catch? Since 2020, hybrid work has left desks half-empty on Mondays and Fridays. Fewer bodies in the building mean fewer daytime porter hours and less tag work. ABM has defended B&I's 7.7% segment margin by focusing on trophy Class A towers and booming sports stadiums, but the segment is swimming against a secular tide.

Now walk into a completely different building: a semiconductor fabrication plant in Arizona or an automated e-commerce distribution hub in Texas. That is Manufacturing & Distribution, ABM's $1.62 billion margin leader at 9.4%. Here, a dirty floor or a miscalibrated air handler isn't an aesthetic annoyance—it can halt a million-dollar-per-hour assembly line or ruin an entire batch of silicon wafers. With the February 2026 acquisition of WGNSTAR, ABM's technicians are embedded inside cleanrooms, managing specialized production tools and ultra-pure environments. Customers do not switch vendors over a 2% price discount when operational continuity is on the line.

Next, step onto the tarmac at Los Angeles International Airport or London Heathrow. Aviation is a $1.12 billion business that moves at the pace of global air travel. ABM runs remote employee parking lots, shuttles passengers between terminals, cleans aircraft cabins, and supports baggage operations. Because airports are heavily unionized and public authorities tender contracts on razor-sharp bids, Aviation carries ABM's lowest segment margin at 5.8%. Yet it is also a volume powerhouse: as passenger traffic surged and the Heathrow contract ramped up in fiscal 2026, Aviation posted 20% growth in Q2 and 12.5% growth in Q3.

Then there is Technical Solutions—the $960.6 million engineering engine at 9.0% margins where ABM's future narrative lives. Imagine a hyperscale data center or a national retail chain that cannot wait three years for a local electric utility to upgrade a substation. ABM's RavenVolt unit designs and builds an on-site hybrid microgrid—combining natural gas generators, battery storage, and custom switchgear—so the facility can 'island' itself from the grid at will. Meanwhile, Quality Uptime Services technicians maintain the uninterruptible power supplies that keep AI servers humming. It is high-skill, high-margin work, though unlike janitorial contracts, EPC project revenue arrives in lumpy waves whenever a customer delays site permitting.

Finally, round out the tour at a sprawling public school district or state university campus—ABM's $922.0 million Education segment at 7.3% margins. Forged largely from the 2017 GCA Services deal, Education is the ultimate steady eddy: schools open every August, gyms need waxing every summer, and superintendents happily outsource custodial and groundskeeping headaches on multi-year contracts.

book_subsections.title: The Corporate Overhead Tax
paragraphs: There is one critical catch you must notice in ABM's segment table. If you add up the operating profits of all five segments in FY2025, you get $687.7 million—a respectable 6.7% segment margin. Yet consolidated GAAP operating profit was only $325.2 million (3.7%). Where did the other $262.5 million go? Corporate unallocated expenses totaled $370.5 million, covering enterprise IT, the ELEVATE ERP rollout, centralized HR/payroll for 113,000 workers, legal, and insurance.

That gap between segment-level profitability (6.7%) and enterprise-level profitability (3.7%) is the central operational puzzle of ABM Industries. Scale helps ABM win national contracts, but managing a decentralized army of 113,000 frontline workers requires a massive corporate superstructure. Until corporate overhead grows significantly slower than segment revenue, or high-margin technical verticals like M&D and Technical Solutions become a much larger share of the pie, consolidated operating margins will remain structurally compressed.

Think about the math in plain terms: if B&I stays sluggish at 0% to 2% growth because of hybrid office work, ABM has to grow M&D and Technical Solutions at double-digit rates just to move the consolidated margin needle by 20 or 30 basis points a year. That is why every investor watching ABM should spend as much time tracking segment mix and corporate expense leverage as they do celebrating headline revenue records.

book_subsections.title: Walking the Floor: Why Mix Shift Matters Across Five Segments
paragraphs: When you walk through ABM's five operating segments, you quickly realize that not all facility dollars are created equal. A standard Class A office janitorial contract in Business & Industry is fiercely competitive, priced per square foot, and vulnerable to tenant downsizing or municipal minimum-wage hikes. Even when ABM wins a multi-year renewal, the margin ceiling is tight.

Now contrast that with an ABM technician servicing a semiconductor cleanroom for WGNSTAR in Oregon or commissioning a RavenVolt microgrid switchgear package for a logistics hub in Texas. In those technical engagements, downtime costs the customer tens of thousands of dollars per hour. The buyer isn't shopping for the cheapest hourly labor rate; they are paying for uptime, regulatory compliance, and specialized engineering certifications. That is why the 10.6% Technical Solutions slice and the semiconductor/biopharma pockets inside Manufacturing & Distribution carry disproportionate importance for ABM's future margin profile.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Look at the contrast between M&D (9.4% margin) and Aviation (5.8% margin), and then look at that $370.5 million corporate overhead line. ABM has built five capable operating engines, but the corporate chassis connecting them is heavy. In Chapter 3, we will dissect the contracts, union rules, and ERP plumbing that determine how much of a revenue dollar actually survives to free cash flow.
